We identify AI-specific security risks organized by international standards and industry associations, and based on these risks, incorporate security-related items into the AI Ethics Checklist and the Guidelines for the Use of Generative AI. This ensures that appropriate security measures are implemented when using AI.
i. The Information Security Division assesses cybersecurity risks in accordance with the Cybersecurity Management Guidelines of the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, and formulates organizational security policies and measures that also take into account emerging external threat trends. These policies are disseminated from headquarters to the security promotion divisions at each business site, which in turn implement security measures at their respective sites.
ii. We have established a Confidential Information Management System under which all information handled internally, including valuable IP and trade secrets, is classified by confidentiality level, and strict management is applied across the entire data lifecycle—including acquisition, storage, use, transfer, and disposal—according to the defined confidentiality levels. For systems, IT equipment, and cloud services (including AI) that handle such confidential information, security and data protection measures are assessed prior to use, and only data permitted by the level of protective measures in place is allowed to be handled, thereby ensuring data protection.
iii. We proactively collect information on external vulnerabilities. For high-urgency vulnerability information, company-wide instructions for countermeasures and inspections are issued and implemented. In addition, software configuration information of systems is registered and managed so that when software vulnerability information is published, affected systems can be identified and prompt information sharing and countermeasure instructions can be provided to the relevant system administrators, in collaboration with relevant stakeholders as needed.
iv. We conduct regular reviews of security measures at least once a year; however, when security incidents occur or highly urgent vulnerabilities are reported, we also carry out ad-hoc reviews of measures and implement emergency responses as necessary.
v. To prevent insider misconduct, we have implemented filtering functions for the external transmission of digital data and access to external content, and system logs are recorded within internal IT systems to enable forensic response. In addition, we have established an internal whistleblowing system, and mutual monitoring among employees further contributes to the prevention of insider misconduct.

Jus Mundi does not currently rely on a single quantitative threshold to determine when an AI-related risk becomes “unreasonable.” Instead, severe AI risks are assessed through a risk-based governance process aligned with the organization’s role as a legal intelligence and technology provider, and with its broader security, privacy, compliance and AI governance frameworks. The most relevant references are ISO/IEC 42001, ISO 27001, the EU AI Act, OECD AI Principles, data protection requirements, and internal information security and risk management policies.
A risk may be considered unreasonable or intolerable when, after considering available mitigations, it could create a severe impact on individuals, clients, the legal process, confidentiality, security, regulatory compliance, or the integrity of Jus Mundi’s services. Examples include: unauthorized disclosure or processing of confidential legal or personal data; AI outputs that could materially mislead users in legal research or decision-making if presented without appropriate caveats or human review; system behavior that could compromise the availability, integrity or security of the platform; discriminatory or unfair outputs in sensitive contexts; or autonomous actions performed without adequate authorization, traceability or human oversight.
In practice, Jus Mundi evaluates these risks using decision criteria such as severity of potential harm, likelihood, scale of exposure, sensitivity of the data involved, reversibility of harm, detectability, regulatory impact, customer impact, and the effectiveness of controls. Risks that remain high or critical after mitigation require escalation to the relevant governance bodies and accountable functions, including Security, Legal/DPO, Product, Engineering and AI governance stakeholders. Deployment may be blocked, delayed, limited to a controlled environment, or subject to additional safeguards where residual risk is not acceptable.
Mitigations are graduated according to the capability and risk profile of the AI system. Lower-risk use cases may require standard controls such as documentation, user guidance, access control, logging, human review and monitoring. Higher-risk use cases may require enhanced review, security and privacy assessments, vendor due diligence, model or application testing, stricter access restrictions, output validation, contractual safeguards, phased deployment, incident response procedures and formal approval before release.
For generative AI, Jus Mundi pays particular attention to hallucination, explainability, source attribution, confidentiality, prompt/input handling, copyright and data protection risks, and user reliance on AI-generated outputs. For agentic AI or tool-using systems, additional scrutiny is applied to autonomy, permissions, ability to take actions, access to sensitive systems or data, auditability, rollback capacity, and human-in-the-loop controls. Agentic capabilities would be restricted or prohibited where they could perform high-impact actions without appropriate authorization, monitoring, and intervention mechanisms. Jus Mundi uses a risk-based approval process before deploying AI systems. Decision authority depends on the risk level and involves the Product and Engineering owners, with Security, Legal/DPO, and AI governance review where confidentiality, privacy, compliance, customer impact, or service integrity may be affected.
Before release, the team reviews the intended use, data involved, vendor or model assessment, security and privacy risks, testing results, output quality, robustness, misuse scenarios, access controls, monitoring, and compliance requirements. Deployment is allowed only when performance is acceptable for the intended use, critical risks are mitigated, and the residual risk is within the organization’s risk appetite.
Higher-risk or customer-facing systems require additional sign-off and may be escalated to governance bodies. Required safeguards may include human oversight, access controls, data minimization, logging, user guidance, source attribution, monitoring, incident response, rollback mechanisms, and phased deployment. For agentic AI, Jus Mundi applies stricter controls on autonomy, permissions, approval gates, audit trails, and the ability to suspend unsafe behavior.

A core component of our measurement approach to responsible AI is running evaluations for frontier models and applications. These evaluations primarily focus on known risks, in contrast to red-teaming, which focuses on known and unknown risks. 
A subset of the mapped risks mentioned in our previous answer is relevant to test at the frontier model level. We evaluate the models for risks such as self-proliferation, offensive cybersecurity, child safety harms, and persuasion. 
Multi-layered red-teaming plays a critical role in our approach, with both internal and external teams proactively testing AI systems for weaknesses and identifying emerging risks. Red-teaming exercises, conducted both internally and externally, proactively assess AI systems for weaknesses and areas for improvement. Teams working on these exercises collaborate to promote information sharing and industry alignment in red-teaming standards. 
Our AI Red Team combines security and AI expertise to simulate attackers who might target AI systems. Based on threat intelligence from teams like the Google Threat Intelligence Group, the AI Red Team explores and identifies how AI features can cause security issues, recommends improvements, and helps ensure that real-world attackers are detected and thwarted before they cause damage. 
Our Content Adversarial Red Team (CART) proactively identifies weaknesses in our AI systems, enabling us to mitigate risks before product launch. Our internal AI tools also assist human expert red teamers and increase the number of attacks they’re able to test for. 
Our external red-teaming includes live hacking events such as DEF CON and Escal8, targeted research grants, challenges, and vulnerability rewards programs to complement our internal evaluations. 
To enhance our approach, we have developed forms of AI-assisted red-teaming – training AI agents to find potential vulnerabilities in other AI systems, drawing on work from gaming breakthroughs like AlphaGo. For example, we recently shared details of how we used AI-assisted red-teaming to understand how vulnerable our systems may be to indirect prompt injection attacks, and to inform how we mitigate the risk. 
Application evaluations are designed to assess the extent to which a given application follows the frameworks and policies that apply to that application. This pre-launch testing generally covers a wide range of risks spanning safety, privacy, and security, and this portfolio of testing results helps inform launch decisions. We also invest in systematic post-launch testing that can take different forms, such as running regression testing for evaluating an application’s ongoing alignment with our frameworks and policies, and cross-product evaluations to identify whether known risks for one application may have manifested in other applications. Yes. We augment our own research by working with external domain experts and trusted testers who can help further our mapping and understanding of risks. 
External evaluations, where appropriate, are conducted by independent external groups on our frontier models. The design of these evaluations is independent and results are reported periodically to the internal team and governance groups. Results are used to mitigate risks and improve evaluation approaches internally. For Gemini 1.5, for example, external groups, including domain experts and a government body, designed their own methodology to test topics within a particular domain area. The time dedicated to testing also varies per group, with some groups working full-time on executing testing processes, while others dedicated one to two days per week. Some groups pursue manual red-teaming and report on qualitative findings from their exploration of model behavior, while others develop bespoke automatic testing strategies and produce quantitative reports of their results. 
We continue to invest in independent research on AI risks. For example, we co-created an AI Safety Fund, initially funded with $10 million to support independent researchers from around the world (academic institutions, research institutions, startups, etc.). The goal of the fund is to allow researchers to better evaluate and understand frontier systems, and – ultimately – develop new model evaluations and techniques for red-teaming AI models.
As described in our response to question 1.d., we signed a first-of-its-kind agreement with fellow members of the Frontier Model Forum (FMF), designed to facilitate information-sharing about threats, vulnerabilities, and capability advances unique to frontier AI. We take a full-stack approach to AI governance – from responsible model development and deployment to post-launch monitoring and remediation. Our policies and principles guide our decision-making, with clear requirements at the pre- and post-launch stages, leadership reviews, and documentation. 
Our governance process is grounded in our principles and frameworks, including:
Our AI Principles, which we established and evolved to guide our approach to developing and deploying AI models and applications, focus on pursuing AI efforts where the likely overall benefits substantially outweigh the foreseeable risks. 
The Frontier Safety Framework, which we recently updated, helps us to proactively prepare for potential risks posed by more powerful frontier AI models. The Framework follows the emerging approach of Responsible Capability Scaling proposed by the U.K.’s AI Safety Institute. 
Our policies for mitigating harm in areas such as child safety, suicide, and self-harm have been informed by years of research, user feedback, and expert consultation. These policies guide our models and products to minimize certain types of harmful outputs.
Our Secure AI Framework focuses on the security and privacy dimensions of AI. 
Additional policies address design, safety, and prohibited uses. 
We operationalize our principles, frameworks, and policies through a system of launch requirements, leadership reviews, and post-launch requirements designed to support continuous improvement. For example, Google DeepMind Responsibility and Safety Council (RSC), Google DeepMind’s governance body, reviews the initial ethics and safety assessments on novel model capabilities in order to provide feedback and guidance during model development. The RSC also reviews data on the model’s performance via assurance evaluations and RSC decisions inform releases.

Through our Frontier Model Forum membership, along with other member firms, we have signed a first-of-its-kind agreement designed to facilitate information-sharing about threats, vulnerabilities, and capability advances unique to frontier AI. This includes risks such as data poisoning, model exfiltration, and rogue actions. We apply security controls, or repeatable mitigations, to these risks. For example, for prompt injections and jailbreaks, we apply robust filtering and processing of inputs and outputs. Additionally, thorough training, tuning, and evaluation processes help fortify the model against prompt injection attacks. For data poisoning, we implement data sanitization, secure AI systems, enable access controls, and deploy mechanisms to ensure data and model integrity.
g.i. We embrace an open and collaborative approach to cybersecurity – working with partners to combine cyber threat intelligence, contribute to AI research, and provide developer tools such as through our AI Cyber Defense Initiative.

g.iii. As mentioned in previous responses, we maintain a Vulnerability Reward Program.

Salesforce scores risks using an automated due diligence framework that classifies products as either lower risk or higher risk. Mitigations are graduated based on these thresholds:
Lower-Risk Products: Teams are fast-tracked and provided with detailed self-service enablement to develop AI in line with legal and ethical requirements
Higher-Risk Products: These require deep human review. The Responsible AI and Technology team initiates kick-off meetings, conducts thorough risk assessments, evaluates the impact with and without mitigations, and requires re-testing post-mitigation. 
Salesforce utilizes an automated due diligence framework that classifies AI products as lower or higher risk. This process is led by Responsible AI and Tech (RAIT) product managers within the Office of Ethical and Humane Use (OEHU).
Threshold Definitions: Risks are identified and categorized under specific sociotechnical harm subtypes. We define unreasonable risk as any unmitigated output that results in catastrophic damage, individualized professional advice (medical/legal/financial) without human review, or the prediction of protected characteristics.
ExploitAI Framework: Our Security team performs ExploitAI activities to uncover AI-specific vulnerabilities, including hallucination exploitation, knowledge poisoning, and multi-agent exploitation.
Empirical Success: Through these pre-launch assessments, we have successfully reduced toxic or unsafe outputs by 35% in specific AI features and decreased biased outputs in partner-integrated content from 69% to 4%. Salesforce mandates that all internal and customer-facing AI products undergo ethics reviews before they can be released to the market. The decision-making process follows a standardized flow:
Intake & Triage: Product teams submit targeted intake forms, which are automatically scored to designate the product as lower or higher risk.
Review & Testing: For higher-risk products, Responsible AI product managers initiate a deep evaluation, categorizing risk scenarios both with and without mitigations. The Testing, Evaluation, and Alignment team conducts tests using both qualitative expert judgment and quantitative industry thresholds.
Implementation & Re-testing: Product teams must implement identified technical and non-technical mitigations, and the product must be re-tested post-mitigation before deployment.
Governance and Approvals Oversight and sign-off authority are distributed across dedicated governance bodies. The Salesforce internal AI Trust Council, composed of senior executives from engineering, legal, security, and ethics, accelerates decision-making for AI products. Internal AI tools require sign-off from the Internal AI Governance Review team. Ultimately, the Chief Ethical and Humane Use Officer reports directly to the C-Suite, and the Board of Directors’ Cybersecurity and Privacy Committee is primarily responsible for reviewing AI strategies, policies, and priorities. Responsibility is distributed across the following key teams and roles:
The AI Council: A cross-functional executive body that serves as the ultimate authority for AI governance. It brings together leaders from Legal, Security, and Product to oversee internal Case Reviews and approve high-risk AI agent deployments.
Office of Ethical and Humane Use (OEHU): This team is responsible for the ethical dimension of secure testing. They lead Consequence Scanning workshops and define the Ethical AI Maturity Model used to validate that AI systems are inclusive, transparent, and safe before they move from staging to production.
Global Security Operations (SecOps): The technical Security Lead role resides here, overseeing the infrastructure for Red-Teaming, adversarial testing, and vulnerability management. They ensure that test environments remain isolated and that the Einstein Trust Layer guardrails (like toxicity filtering and data masking) are functioning correctly.
Product and Engineering Teams: Individual AI System Owners within specific product units (e.g., Service Cloud, Sales Cloud) are accountable for the day-to-day performance and security of their models. They are responsible for implementing the human-in-the-loop controls and continuous monitoring required by the AI Council.
Data Governance & Privacy Teams: These teams oversee the AI-safe data lifecycle, ensuring that synthetic or anonymized datasets are used during testing and that Zero Data Retention policies are technically enforced.
Shared Responsibility Structure
This is not a siloed function; rather, it is an interdependent framework. While the Security team provides the secure environment (infrastructure), the OEHU provides the ethical rubric (policy), and the Product teams provide the technical execution (testing). All three must certify a system's readiness through the Model Registry before it is authorized for global deployment.

Following deployment, Salesforce uses a dedicated Ethical Use Policy team to manage case operations, content safety, and user escalations. Workspace users in regions like the EU can use in-product reporting tools (e.g., Report to Slack) to flag prohibited or illegal content, which is then reviewed around the clock by specialists. 
The Policy team uses these reports and stakeholder engagement to actively identify emerging risks, potential harms, or policy gaps. These insights trigger a rigorous update process for customer-facing guidelines; for example, the AI Acceptable Use Policy (AUP) is continuously refined as risks and technologies evolve. Additionally, to trigger rapid corrective action for broader security issues, Salesforce employs an AI-powered incident response system that automatically triages next steps based on case descriptions, saving thousands of hours and evaluating incident response quality. Salesforce operationalizes mechanisms to receive reports of risk and misuse directly from our users. To comply with the European Union’s Digital Services Act (DSA), we introduced in-product reporting capabilities, including the Report to Slack option, which allows workspace users in the EU to seamlessly flag prohibited or illegal content. The Ethical Use Policy team and its global Operations specialists actively manage these user escalations, working around the clock to assess reports against safety standards and the company's AUPs. Salesforce utilizes a coordinated system to track, manage, and learn from incidents across its AI lifecycle:
Internal Tracking Systems: The Policy Operations function within the Office of Ethical and Humane Use manages specialized case management and content safety operations. These operations include responding to user reports and maintaining detailed documentation of incident timelines and outcomes.
Incident Logs and Audit Trails: Technical safeguards, such as the Einstein Trust Layer, automatically log toxicity scores and interaction data into an audit trail stored in Data 360. These logs visualize toxicity trends over time, providing a verifiable record of system behavior for internal review.
Root-Cause Analysis: Salesforce’s incident response team uses Agentforce to automatically triage next steps for security incidents and evaluate the quality of responses. This process includes conducting post-incident analysis to identify the root cause of an issue and areas where technical or non-technical mitigations (such as updated Trust Patterns) are required.
Escalation Thresholds:Strategic Escalation: Salesforce defines clear paths for surfacing high-impact incidents to senior leadership, including the Cybersecurity and Privacy Committee of the Board of Directors and the AI Trust Council.
Automated Thresholds: Escalation is often encoded directly into the system; for example, high-stakes situations involving regulatory compliance, significant financial exposure, or agent uncertainty automatically trigger a transfer to human review.
Policy Escalation: Concerns related to high-priority ethical use cases follow a structured process where recommendations are presented to executive leadership for final review and approval.

Prior to deploying AI systems, we implement the following measures from a multifaceted perspective, including AI governance, quality control, and security.
1. Risk Assessment Based on AI Governance and Human Rights Policies
In accordance with the “NEC Group AI and Human Rights Principles,” we conduct risk assessments using risk checklists and implement countermeasures at every phase of the lifecycle—from planning and proposal through design and development to operation and maintenance. Additionally, based on the “AI Guidelines for Business,” we apply and update these guidelines within our internal AI governance framework.
2. Development Management and Quantitative Standards Based on the AI Quality Guidelines
To ensure the quality of AI-powered systems, we have been applying the “NEC AI Quality Guidelines,” established in December 2019, to development projects since April 2020. These guidelines establish specific standards and checklists for each of the four development phases (1. System Planning and Proof of Concept (PoC), 2. Data Collection and Processing, 3. Model Creation, Evaluation, and Testing, and 4. System Operation). By conducting checks when transitioning between phases, we proactively prevent risks in the subsequent phase. In particular, by setting quantitative standards for the volume of training data, as well as for outliers and missing values, we ensure clarity in these standards and enable objective assessments by third parties.
3. Evaluation and Safety Measures for the Generative AI Core Technology “cotomi” and AI Agents

Internal rules, such as the “NEC AI Quality Guidelines,” are updated regularly (e.g., to enhance the checklist for generative AI), and we have established “recognition of new threats arising from technological advancements” and “changes in the social environment” as triggers for these updates (e.g., we have updated our policies in response to the increased risk of copyright infringement in image-generation services).

To maintain the safety and reliability of our AI models and systems and to mitigate risks, we operate an integrated framework that encompasses the collection and analysis of incident and threat information, vulnerability management, industry and global collaboration, post-deployment operations and customer support, and quality improvement.
1. Deployment of AI Models and Systems
We have established a CSIRT (Computer Security Incident Response Team) under the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) to monitor cyberattacks, analyze the characteristics of attacks and malware, preserve and analyze data in the event of an incident, investigate the causes, and resolve the situation.
2. Provision of AI Models and Systems
Through the “Cyber Intelligence Sharing Platform,” we rapidly share threat intelligence—including cyberattack methods, incident cases, vulnerability risk metrics, and security countermeasure indicators—with each business division, where it is utilized as a basis for assessing business risks.
In addition, we have established the NEC Group Information Security Incident Response Desk, which receives and manages reports of security incidents. The desk includes experts in security, legal affairs, and public relations, who provide response advice from various perspectives. By operating a system that collects vulnerability information regarding products and customer deliverables and distributes patch information, we ensure a rapid response to newly identified vulnerabilities and incorporate these findings into the revision of our guidelines.
For post-deployment maintenance and operational support, we maintain and operate programs that monitor logs and implement countermeasures appropriate to the level of risk. Furthermore, we have established it as standard company practice to report and explain issues to each customer using our AI systems and to implement improvements when problems are confirmed. We participate in the “AI Safety Evaluation Environment Task Force” operated by Japan AISI, sharing insights and providing feedback within the industry based on our trial use of AI safety evaluation tools, including automated red-team functions. Based on a company-wide cybersecurity governance framework overseen by the CISO (Chief Information Security Officer) and compliance with international standards and specifications, we implement the following security measures for AI (Security for AI) and multi-layered protection measures for high-value and highly confidential AI assets:
1. Company-wide Cybersecurity Governance Framework, Standards, and Shared Infrastructure
Based on the “NEC Group Information Security Statement,” the “Basic Information Security Rules,” and the “Cybersecurity Management Rules,” we have clarified our accountability structure to establish and maintain the ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001), and we implement security measures for customer-facing systems, products, and services. Under the oversight of the CISO, the CSIRT (comprising four teams: Threat Intelligence, Incident Response, SOC, and Development) is responsible for monitoring, analyzing, and investigating cyberattacks to determine their causes. PSIRT operates a vulnerability information management system and a permanently open reporting channel (psirt-info[at]mlsig.jp.nec.com), and publishes response information under an early warning partnership with JPCERT/CC and other organizations. We have also established a framework for collaboration between the cybersecurity department and the information security administrators in each business division.
We comply with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0, ISO/IEC 27001, and the “Cybersecurity Management Guidelines Ver. 3.0.” We conduct quarterly (four times a year) vulnerability assessments, review countermeasures twice a year at information security strategy meetings, and perform regular cyber risk assessments by a Red Team.
We have implemented multi-factor authentication, passwordless authentication, EDR/NDR, DLP, and file encryption company-wide based on the Zero Trust Model (CISA Maturity Model).
2. Security Measures for AI (Security for AI)
We are systematically advancing our efforts along three pillars: “Governance (Establishing Policies and Rules),” “Management (Reviewing and visualizing compliance requirements),” and “Security Infrastructure (AI Asset Detection = Shadow AI Detection, AI Vulnerability Assessments and Audits, AI Guardrails).”
Referencing Japan AISI’s “Guide to Red Teaming Methodology on AI Safety” and the OWASP AI Testing Guide, we conduct verification of attack scenarios—such as prompt injection (direct and indirect) and jailbreak—in a controlled, isolated environment, while also performing penetration testing on systems, including large language models (LLMs). Additionally, we have set the automation of attack diagnostics by the AI Red Team as one of our key objectives.
For “NEC Generative AI Service,” used internally, we have implemented prompt input restrictions based on information confidentiality classifications, as well as a system that logs all input and output in a manner that allows for continuous auditing.
The mandatory cybersecurity checklist includes items specific to AI systems, and we are implementing the necessary measures for each project.
3. Special Protective Measures for Highly Confidential and Valuable AI Assets (Training Data, Models, Inference Environments, etc.)
Sensitive AI assets (such as data, model weights, and inference environments) are managed using secure storage (access control, encryption, and audit trail management) and are provided in on-premises or dedicated cloud environments within a dedicated data center. This ensures that access to high-value AI assets is restricted to a controlled environment, including through secure, private connections to public clouds.
We are working to ensure confidentiality at the hardware level by running “cotomi” inference on a confidential computing environment (using a Trusted Execution Environment, or TEE). Conduct post-deployment monitoring
Perform root-cause analysis and apply lessons learned to improve future development and/or deployment practices
Monitoring and emergency controls specific to agentic AI systems (e.g., ability to interrupt autonomous action sequences, override tool-use permissions, or revoke delegated authority)

If an incident occurs that is suspected to be a security incident, we report it to the NEC Group Information Security Incident Response Desk. Integration Across the AI System Lifecycle
Our risk management practices operate together in a continuous feedback loop:
We take a research-driven, scientific approach to identify current and emerging risks across new modalities, codifying these inputs into a risk taxonomy.
We proactively address risks through rigorous guidelines—such as content safety policies, the Prohibited Use Policy, the Secure AI Framework, and the Frontier Safety Framework—intended to prevent harmful outputs and guide model behavior.
We stress-test systems against these frameworks using scaled evaluations alongside internal and external red-teaming.
We mitigate identified risks through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and out-of-model mitigations like safety filters and conditional system instructions.
Post-launch, we use automated systems and human reviews to monitor for misuse.
We have mature incident management and crisis response capabilities to rapidly mitigate and remediate where needed, and feed this back into our risk identification efforts.
Cross-Cutting Governance, Review, and Escalation Processes Our governance process is grounded in a system of cross-cutting governance bodies and review forums to manage escalations and approve launches.
Our multi-layered process includes launch reviews for both frontier models and applications developed using these models.
Model releases are specifically approved by Google DeepMind’s Launch Review forum, while application launches are reviewed via centralized expert risk reviews and application-focused forums.
For long-term and structural risks, our AGI Futures Council—consisting of senior management and Alphabet’s Board of Directors—provides perspectives and recommendations to our Board and management team on long-term opportunities, risks, and impacts associated with the development of AGI.
Frequency of Reviews and Trigger Events
Our risk management practices are fundamentally iterative.
Our approach evolves with developments in the underlying technology, new and emerging risks, and as new measurement techniques emerge, such as AI-assisted evaluations.
To assess whether a model contributes to identified safety risks, we conduct a critical capability assessment against Threshold/Critical Capability Levels (T/CCLs) prior to its initial external deployment. For subsequent model iterations, we execute material capability change assessments during post-training—evaluating specific checkpoints based on provenance, size, modality, and benchmark performance—to identify meaningful capability increases that could alter our risk determination. This monitoring relies on "early warning evaluations" and defined "alert thresholds"—mechanisms designed to flag when a Critical Capability Level (CCL) may be reached before a full critical capability assessment is repeated—which can be dynamically adjusted or run more frequently if the observed rate of progress diminishes our established safety buffers.
Our Frontier Safety Framework will be reviewed at least once a year—more frequently if we have reasonable grounds to believe the adequacy of the Framework or our adherence to it has been materially undermined. The process will involve (i) an assessment of the Framework’s appropriateness for the management of significant and severe risk, drawing on information sources such as record of adherence to the framework, relevant high-quality research, information shared through industry forums, and evaluation results, as necessary, and (ii) an assessment of our adherence to the Framework.
Distinctions Between Types of AI Systems
We proactively assess and tailor our risk management approach based on the specific type and capability of the AI system:
Frontier AI Models: Governed by the Frontier Safety Framework, which is built around capability thresholds called Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) intended to address severe risks like misuse and deceptive alignment.
Agentic AI & Personal Intelligence: In this agentic era—where AI systems autonomously interact with services and users—we require a new testing paradigm; our Novel AI Testing team was formed to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems, such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.
Artificial General Intelligence (AGI): Managed with a focus on long-term, structural risks, exploring four main risk areas—misuse, misalignment, accidents, and structural risks—under the guidance of the AGI Futures Council and the approach detailed in Google Deepmind’s AGI Safety paper. Our governance process is grounded in a multi-layered oversight structure to govern secure testing throughout the AI system lifecycle. Responsibility is distributed across specialized central functions, creative red-teaming units, and senior governance councils:
Central Security and Reliability Teams: Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our own infrastructure, where we apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle—supported by central security teams and a security, safety, and reliability organization consisting of engineers and researchers with world-class expertise.
Frontier Model Testing & External Partnerships: For model-level frontier testing, the Google DeepMind Responsibility Team operates directly within model development. Their core mission is to proactively track emerging risks, conduct structural safety evaluations (such as red-teaming), and align future models with ethical frameworks before deployment. Additionally, we work with external expert organizations through our External Safety Testing Program. These experts independently test and provide feedback on frontier safety domains. The team also actively collaborates with independent groups like the U.K. AI Security Institute and is a founding member of the Frontier Model Forum.
Application Testing: At the application/product level, our Content Adversarial Red Team (CART) proactively identifies unknown risks in our AI systems, enabling us to mitigate before launch. To evaluate our most advanced frontier systems, our Novel AI Testing team was formed to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems, such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.
Security-focused red teaming: Our AI Red Team combines security and AI expertise to simulate attackers who might target AI systems; based on threat intelligence from teams like the Google Threat Intelligence Group, this unit explores how AI features can cause security issues, recommends improvements, and helps ensure that real-world attackers are detected and thwarted before they cause damage.
Governance Councils: Our model launches are reviewed at Google DeepMind’s Launch Review forum, which approves model releases, and our many application launches are reviewed systematically via launch infrastructure and centralized expert risk reviews, as well as via various application-focused launch review forums. These launch-specific forums are complemented by our Artificial General Intelligence (AGI) Futures Council, which consists of members of senior management and our Board of Directors.
Technical Description of Security Measures in Testing
Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we pursue AI responsibly by grounding our testing processes in the systematic application of technical controls to isolate risks and rigorously validate frontier models prior to deployment.
Testing Environments and Target Isolation Testing is performed in appropriately secured environments. Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our infrastructure, where we can apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle, ensuring that any external trusted testing groups also receive secure access to test models. To address the safety and scalability challenges inherent in live internet testing of agentic products, where appropriate, we either restrict internet access during evals or require human-in-the-loop approval. This allows us to proactively identify and mitigate high harm risks without exposing the public web to potential harm. Additionally, we mandate that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments. A gradual approach to deployment serves as a critical risk mitigation—starting with testing internally, then releasing to trusted testers externally, before opening up to a small portion of our user base.
Containment, Capability Restrictions, and Controls To protect frontier models against adversarial inputs, we deploy robust cybersecurity controls and repeatable mitigations. For prompt injections and jailbreaks, we apply robust filtering and processing of inputs and outputs, while thorough training, tuning, and evaluation processes help fortify the model against these attacks. For data poisoning, we implement data sanitization, secure AI systems, enable access controls, and deploy mechanisms to ensure data and model integrity.
Agentic systems require a multi-layer defense strategy. We employ a hybrid defense-in-depth strategy that combines deterministic measures with dynamic, reasoning-based defenses to achieve a layered safety and security strategy. For example, in Chrome, we use a combination of rule-based and LLM-based approaches to limit agents permitted actions. This mechanism vets agents' actions against the user’s stated goal, rejecting misaligned steps. Ultimately, this comprehensive strategy combines human-in-the-loop expertise with AI-assisted scale to enable data-driven safety and security assessments.
Audit Logging, Monitoring, and Test-Data Curation We maintain oversight during evaluations by implementing automated monitoring agents that log interactions and assess the compliance of the agent being tested in real-time in certain contexts. Automatic testing for security vulnerabilities helps us assess code risks dynamically. To optimize test-data quality by design, we use automated techniques to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets. Furthermore, we invest in "few shot" learning methodologies where an AI creates a synthetic testing set based on inputs from experts—significantly accelerating the testing scale when compared with the manual human creation of testing sets.

We proactively address risks through rigorous guidelines—such as content safety policies, the Prohibited Use Policy, the Secure AI Framework, and the Frontier Safety Framework—intended to prevent harmful outputs and guide model behavior.
We stress-test systems against these frameworks using scaled evaluations alongside internal and external red-teaming.
We mitigate identified risks through supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and out-of-model mitigations like safety filters and conditional system instructions.
Post-launch, we use automated systems and human reviews to monitor for misuse.
We have mature incident management and crisis response capabilities to rapidly mitigate and remediate where needed, and feed this back into our risk identification efforts.

Our multi-layered process includes launch reviews for both frontier models and applications developed using these models.
Model releases are specifically approved by Google DeepMind’s Launch Review forum, while application launches are reviewed via centralized expert risk reviews and application-focused forums.
For long-term and structural risks, our AGI Futures Council—consisting of senior management and Alphabet’s Board of Directors—provides perspectives and recommendations to our Board and management team on long-term opportunities, risks, and impacts associated with the development of AGI.
Frequency of Reviews and Trigger Events
Our risk management practices are fundamentally iterative.
Our approach evolves with developments in the underlying technology, new and emerging risks, and as new measurement techniques emerge, such as AI-assisted evaluations.
To assess whether a model contributes to identified safety risks, we conduct a critical capability assessment against Threshold/Critical Capability Levels (T/CCLs) prior to its initial external deployment. For subsequent model iterations, we execute material capability change assessments during post-training—evaluating specific checkpoints based on provenance, size, modality, and benchmark performance—to identify meaningful capability increases that could alter our risk determination. This monitoring relies on "early warning evaluations" and defined "alert thresholds"—mechanisms designed to flag when a Critical Capability Level (CCL) may be reached before a full critical capability assessment is repeated—which can be dynamically adjusted or run more frequently if the observed rate of progress diminishes our established safety buffers.

Frontier AI Models: Governed by the Frontier Safety Framework, which is built around capability thresholds called Critical Capability Levels (CCLs) intended to address severe risks like misuse and deceptive alignment.
Agentic AI & Personal Intelligence: In this agentic era—where AI systems autonomously interact with services and users—we require a new testing paradigm; our Novel AI Testing team was formed to spearhead evaluations at scale for new AI systems, such as advanced agents and Personal Intelligence.

Technical Description of Security Measures in Testing
Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we pursue AI responsibly by grounding our testing processes in the systematic application of technical controls to isolate risks and rigorously validate frontier models prior to deployment.
Testing Environments and Target Isolation Testing is performed in appropriately secured environments. Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our infrastructure, where we can apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle, ensuring that any external trusted testing groups also receive secure access to test models. To address the safety and scalability challenges inherent in live internet testing of agentic products, where appropriate, we either restrict internet access during evals or require human-in-the-loop approval. This allows us to proactively identify and mitigate high harm risks without exposing the public web to potential harm. Additionally, we mandate that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments. A gradual approach to deployment serves as a critical risk mitigation—starting with testing internally, then releasing to trusted testers externally, before opening up to a small portion of our user base.
Containment, Capability Restrictions, and Controls To protect frontier models against adversarial inputs, we deploy robust cybersecurity controls and repeatable mitigations. For prompt injections and jailbreaks, we apply robust filtering and processing of inputs and outputs, while thorough training, tuning, and evaluation processes help fortify the model against these attacks. For data poisoning, we implement data sanitization, secure AI systems, enable access controls, and deploy mechanisms to ensure data and model integrity.
Agentic systems require a multi-layer defense strategy. We employ a hybrid defense-in-depth strategy that combines deterministic measures with dynamic, reasoning-based defenses to achieve a layered safety and security strategy. For example, in Chrome, we use a combination of rule-based and LLM-based approaches to limit agents permitted actions. This mechanism vets agents' actions against the user’s stated goal, rejecting misaligned steps. Ultimately, this comprehensive strategy combines human-in-the-loop expertise with AI-assisted scale to enable data-driven safety and security assessments.
Audit Logging, Monitoring, and Test-Data Curation We maintain oversight during evaluations by implementing automated monitoring agents that log interactions and assess the compliance of the agent being tested in real-time in certain contexts. Automatic testing for security vulnerabilities helps us assess code risks dynamically. To optimize test-data quality by design, we use automated techniques to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets. Furthermore, we invest in "few shot" learning methodologies where an AI creates a synthetic testing set based on inputs from experts—significantly accelerating the testing scale when compared with the manual human creation of testing sets.

Identifying Emerging Issues We use numerous internal and external signals including incident reports to identify new risks through continuous post-launch monitoring that leverages both automated systems and human review. We strive to learn from our post-market monitoring mechanisms, including as part of our detection, mitigation, response and/or reporting of incidents related to our AI risk domains. Actionable insights from these processes allow us to enhance our tools, training, processes, policies, and response efforts.

Our residual risk assessments, safety cases and mitigations may be updated as a result of post-market monitoring, including information about incidents and near misses relating to our frontier safety risk domains. Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review and might result in updates to the related residual risk assessment or safety case.

We use a variety of means for taking corrective action tailored to the particular facts of an incident. For example, teams are explicitly enabled to have rapid-remediation mechanisms in place to immediately block content flagged as illegal. Our governance process is grounded in a comprehensive, full-lifecycle approach to AI security, heavily guided by our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) and our AI Principles. Because we understand that advanced AI involves evolving complexities, we proactively integrate AI risks into our broader cybersecurity risk management, utilizing a secure-by-default methodology across the ecosystem.
For particularly sensitive AI assets—such as proprietary and unreleased model weights—we implement specific, heightened measures.
Asset Protection Commitments: We maintain a formal commitment to invest in cybersecurity and insider threat safeguards to protect proprietary and unreleased model weights.
Secure Infrastructure: To ensure the robust protection of these high-value assets, we mandate that our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored exclusively within our own secure infrastructure.
Continuous Monitoring: Within this protected infrastructure, SAIF is applied throughout the AI lifecycle and supported by central security teams—including our Detection & Response team—which provides 24/7/365 monitoring of products, services, and infrastructure, featuring a dedicated team for insider threat and abuse. Post-Deployment Monitoring and Governance Our governance continues post-launch with assessments for issues that might arise across products. Post-launch governance helps us to identify risks, alongside opportunities to improve our models, applications, and our governance processes.
We use a combination of automated systems and human reviews to engage in continuous post-launch monitoring to improve our AI models and products, and detect activity and behavior that suggests misuse of our consumer products. This continuous monitoring ecosystem includes, where relevant, actively soliciting user feedback, evaluating logs data to identify known and emerging user adoption patterns, and monitoring third-party signals via social media and trusted partners. Furthermore, our Detection & Response team provides 24/7/365 monitoring of Google products, services, and infrastructure—featuring a dedicated team for insider threat and abuse.
To proactively assess and identify external vulnerabilities, we also have a Vulnerability Reward Program to specifically encourage the reporting of issues in our AI products. 
Root-Cause Analysis and Incident Remediation We employ mature incident management and crisis response capabilities to rapidly mitigate and remediate where needed, and feed this intelligence back into our risk identification efforts. As a core mechanism of our lifecycle governance, safety cases and mitigations may be updated as a result of post-market monitoring, including information about incidents relating to our frontier safety risk domains. Material updates to a safety case will be submitted to the appropriate governance function for review and might result in updates to the related residual risk assessment or safety case.
Ecosystem Collaboration We are investing in industry-leading approaches to advance safety and security research and benchmarks, pioneering technical solutions to address risks, and sharing our learnings with the ecosystem. For example, through our Frontier Model Forum membership alongside other member firms, we signed an agreement designed to facilitate information-sharing about threats, vulnerabilities, and capability advances unique to frontier AI.

Our incident response programs are managed by teams of expert incident responders across many specialized functions to ensure each response is well-tailored to the challenges presented by each incident.
At the resolution stage, the focus is on investigating the root cause, limiting the impact of the incident, resolving immediate safety, security, or other risks (if any), implementing necessary fixes as part of remediation, and recovering affected systems, data, and services.
Following the successful remediation and resolution of a data incident, the incident response team evaluates the lessons learned from the incident. When the incident raises critical issues, the incident commander might initiate a post-mortem analysis. We strive to learn from every incident and implement preventative measures to avoid future incidents. Actionable insights from incident analysis enable us to enhance our tools, training, processes, overall security and privacy data protection program, security policies, and response efforts.

Technical Description of Security Measures in Testing
Because we understand that AI, as a still-emerging transformative technology, involves evolving complexities and risks, we pursue AI responsibly by grounding our testing processes in the systematic application of technical controls to isolate risks and rigorously validate frontier models prior to deployment.
Testing Environments and Target Isolation Testing is performed in appropriately secured environments. Our frontier models are developed, trained, tested, and stored within our infrastructure, where we can apply our Secure AI Framework (SAIF) throughout the AI lifecycle, ensuring that any external trusted testing groups also receive secure access to test models. To address the safety and scalability challenges inherent in live internet testing of agentic products, where appropriate, we either restrict internet access during evals or require human-in-the-loop approval. This allows us to proactively identify and mitigate high harm risks without exposing the public web to potential harm. Additionally, we mandate that the processing of untrusted inputs occurs within sandboxed environments. A gradual approach to deployment serves as a critical risk mitigation—starting with testing internally, then releasing to trusted testers externally, before opening up to a small portion of our user base.
Containment, Capability Restrictions, and Controls To protect frontier models against adversarial inputs, we deploy robust cybersecurity controls and repeatable mitigations. For prompt injections and jailbreaks, we apply robust filtering and processing of inputs and outputs, while thorough training, tuning, and evaluation processes help fortify the model against these attacks. For data poisoning, we implement data sanitization, secure AI systems, enable access controls, and deploy mechanisms to ensure data and model integrity.
Agentic systems require a multi-layer defense strategy. We employ a hybrid defense-in-depth strategy that combines deterministic measures with dynamic, reasoning-based defenses to achieve a layered safety and security strategy. For example, in Chrome, we use a combination of rule-based and LLM-based approaches to limit agents permitted actions. This mechanism vets agents' actions against the user’s stated goal, rejecting misaligned steps. Ultimately, this comprehensive strategy combines human-in-the-loop expertise with AI-assisted scale to enable data-driven safety and security assessments.
Audit Logging, Monitoring, and Test-Data Curation We maintain oversight during evaluations by implementing automated monitoring agents that log interactions and assess the compliance of the agent being tested in real-time in certain contexts. Automatic testing for security vulnerabilities helps us assess code risks dynamically. To optimize test-data quality by design, we use automated techniques to filter out certain personal information and other sensitive data from training sets. Furthermore, we invest in "few shot" learning methodologies where an AI creates a synthetic testing set based on inputs from experts—significantly accelerating the testing scale when compared with the manual human creation of testing sets. quote:
OpenAI assesses severe frontier AI risks under its published Preparedness Framework and Frontier Governance Framework. The Preparedness Framework establishes risk-specific High and Critical capability thresholds and corresponding safeguards. Covered systems reaching High capability require safeguards that sufficiently minimize the associated risk of severe harm before deployment; systems reaching Critical capability also require such safeguards during development. Capabilities Reports and Safeguards Reports inform review by the Safety Advisory Group, which advises OpenAI leadership. The Frontier Governance Framework describes how relevant safety and security practices align with covered regulatory risks, including risk assessment and mitigation, transparency reporting, security risk management, and incident response.
These frameworks describe capability- and threat-model-specific criteria rather than a single numerical threshold across all AI systems. OpenAI also maintains ISO/IEC 42001 certification for its AI management system and ISO/IEC 27001 certification for in-scope information-security management systems. Our security and privacy page describes the scope of these certifications, which complement the frontier-specific risk governance described above. Plan and design: We identify how a system is intended to be used and what could go wrong, then use that assessment to decide which tests and safeguards are needed.
Collect and process data: We select, prepare and filter training data, applying relevant privacy protections and controls over where data comes from.
Build, integrate and interpret model: We test the model as it is developed and use the findings to improve its behavior and relevant protections.
Verify and validate: We examine what the system can do and safeguards’ effectiveness, using internal automated and human testing and relevant input from outside experts.
Deploy: We review the evidence and the risks that remain after safeguards are applied before deciding whether and how to release the system, which may include phased deployment to understand potential risk among a smaller audience before broadening access.
Operate and monitor: We monitor for misuse and incidents after release and use what we learn to improve safeguards and future assessments.
Evaluations are performed at multiple points throughout the AI lifecycle to ensure models are safe, effective, and align with OpenAI's objectives. In the pre-development phase, we begin with an initial risk assessment to identify potential hazards and define safety objectives, establishing a foundation for informed and responsible development. During the development phase, models undergo iterative testing to refine safety and performance as the model evolves. Before deployment, in the pre-deployment phase, we conduct a range of safety and capability evaluations, as described in our Preparedness Framework. In the deployment phase, we implement system safeguards to prevent harm and monitoring to detect unexpected behaviors or misuse, and we perform post-deployment evaluations using real-world feedback and performance data to identify emerging risks. Finally, in the post-deployment and maintenance phase, we update our evaluations and safeguards based on new misuse patterns, identified incidents, and advances in research.
We embed security controls into infrastructure and model development, and use adversarial testing, monitoring and incident review to improve them. Our work on long-horizon models has also shown why individual action checks alone can be insufficient: a sequence of seemingly acceptable actions can cross a user’s intended boundary.
Significant releases, material evaluation findings, incidents, emerging abuse patterns and changes in applicable requirements can trigger reviews and updates. Findings may change evaluations, model behavior, safeguards, access conditions or monitoring. The Safety Advisory Group advises OpenAI leadership on preparedness decisions, and relevant research, safety, security, product, legal and policy teams contribute according to their responsibilities. An explanation of the safety work for a model is published in a system card when the model is released to general availability.
Findings from internal use, evaluations and incident investigations inform our alignment work, security controls and decisions about whether work can proceed. Our September 25, 2026 report provides a further example of how incident findings change safeguards and research decisions. An internal research model accessed an external chatbot through insufficient DNS filtering in its training sandbox. Monitoring detected the behavior, but the investigation also identified gaps in detection and operational response. We stopped the affected training run and added blocking controls at two independent layers. At time of publication, training, evaluation and tool-using inference for our most capable models were paused pending validation that the gap was resolved and additional red teaming. We also committed to beginning a fresh training run with additional alignment improvements rather than resuming training of the affected model. OpenAI has implemented several AI risk management and governance policies, as described in System Cards, our Preparedness Framework and our Frontier Governance Framework. For example, before deploying frontier models and other significant launches, preparedness evaluations and safeguards are reviewed by the Safety Advisory Group, an internal cross-functional group of safety leaders, with recommendations to OpenAI leadership, which makes deployment decisions. Additionally, the Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation has oversight of safety and security practices across OpenAI.
The Frontier Governance Framework also sets out responsibilities for the activities it covers. It identifies OpenAI OpCo LLC’s responsibilities for covered US models and OpenAI Ireland Limited’s responsibilities for EU general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, including oversight by its board for EU purposes.
OpenAI regularly iterates on other policies and procedures to assess, measure, and mitigate risks throughout the development and deployment lifecycle.
Reviews and updates can be triggered by major incidents, regulatory changes, material system updates and new evaluation findings.

OpenAI employs rigorous red-teaming processes to evaluate the performance of models and systems before external deployment. OpenAI uses both human and automated red-teaming processes. Adversarial testing involves experts who attempt to exploit the model in ways that could cause harm or lead to undesirable outcomes, or who probe the model for unexpected or unwanted behavior in a variety of domains. This process is complemented by collaborations with external organizations, such as cybersecurity firms, to provide additional perspectives and expertise in identifying potential threats.
OpenAI’s red teaming efforts include a variety of expert testing organizations that help inform our risk assessment and mitigation efforts. These organizations span a variety of domains, with diverse perspectives.
Our model review process is also informed by third-party assessments. Since our previous submission, we have published more detail on three forms of external testing: independent capability and safeguard evaluations, reviews of evaluation methodology, and direct probing by subject-matter experts. These assessments supplement our internal work and inform deployment decisions.
We use regression testing to make sure models are robust against previously discovered jailbreaks, and perform new rounds of automated red-teaming with our latest internal red-teaming attackers to validate our improvements.
Red teaming and adversarial testing are used to uncover failure modes, misuse potential, or unexpected behaviors. These findings often lead to downstream mitigation efforts — such as refining instructions, retraining, or introducing product-level safeguards.
The results of these testing activities are documented and reviewed by relevant stakeholders (e.g., model developers, product teams, risk reviewers), and actions are prioritized based on impact, feasibility, and alignment with risk thresholds.
The Safety Advisory Group reviews Capabilities Reports and Safeguards Reports, assesses residual risk and makes recommendations to OpenAI leadership, which makes deployment decisions. Findings can lead to further evaluation, stronger safeguards, access restrictions or a phased release.
We use a combination of quantitative (e.g., internal benchmarks, as well as third-party testers’ evaluations) and qualitative (e.g., subject-matter expert judgment, preparedness review outcomes, stakeholder feedback) metrics to assess AI-related risk. These are embedded in our risk evaluations. We describe some of these metrics, methodologies, and limitations in system cards and in research we publish.
It is worthwhile to note that some risks (e.g., reputational or ethical harm) resist easy quantification, and we lean on expert judgment. AI system behavior can change over time (e.g., through fine-tuning or model evolution), so risks may need ongoing validation. Additionally, risk evaluations are context-sensitive — what is lower-risk in one setting may be higher-risk in another. Risk evaluations are continually re-evaluated based on changes to the threat landscape, and in response to adverse, anomalous, or malicious activity observed on our platform.
For agentic systems, evaluation results also depend on the tools, software environment, scoring method and resources available during testing. We check for issues such as prior exposure to test material, invalid tasks and shortcuts in scoring, and interpret results within the conditions tested. OpenAI has implemented several AI risk management and governance policies, as described in System Cards, our Preparedness Framework and our Frontier Governance Framework. For example, before deploying frontier models and other significant launches, preparedness evaluations and safeguards are reviewed by the Safety Advisory Group, an internal cross-functional group of safety leaders, with recommendations to OpenAI leadership, which makes deployment decisions. Additionally, the Safety and Security Committee of the OpenAI Foundation has oversight of safety and security practices across OpenAI.
The Frontier Governance Framework also sets out responsibilities for the activities it covers. It identifies OpenAI OpCo LLC’s responsibilities for covered US models and OpenAI Ireland Limited’s responsibilities for EU general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, including oversight by its board for EU purposes.
OpenAI regularly iterates on other policies and procedures to assess, measure, and mitigate risks throughout the development and deployment lifecycle.
Reviews and updates can be triggered by major incidents, regulatory changes, material system updates and new evaluation findings.

Question 12 — vulnerability management
OpenAI receives vulnerability reports through its security and safety bounty programs and provides an encrypted channel for reporting security incidents. Its disclosure policy also describes coordination for vulnerabilities found in third-party software and its role as a CVE Numbering Authority. 
For covered frontier systems, security assessments include red teaming, penetration testing and vulnerability scanning.
Question 13 — post-deployment practices
OpenAI disallows the use of our models and tools for certain activities and content, as outlined in our terms and usage policies. These policies are designed to prohibit the use of our models and tools in ways that cause individual or societal harm. We periodically update these policies in response to new risks and new information on how our models are being used. Access to and use of our models are also subject to OpenAI’s Terms of Use and our Business Terms. We employ a combination of guardrails, tools, policies, and processes to detect and enforce against abuse of our models. In addition to usage policies, we employ automated systems (for example, our Moderation API) and AI-powered tools to detect and prevent harmful content, human reviewers and expert investigators to conduct detailed investigations of model behavior and platform abuse, and external input to help our teams iterate on and regularly improve our moderation, detection, disruption, and enforcement capabilities. We publish information related to our post-deployment monitoring, mitigation and enforcement activities.
We build robust monitoring systems to detect potential model misalignment. We view model alignment as the primary lever to prevent potential misaligned behavior from our models. However, monitoring provides broad visibility into frontier model behavior, illuminating opportunities to further improve alignment and safety. This serves as an additional layer of protection against misaligned behavior that is detected.
Addressing vulnerabilities, incidents, emerging risks and misuse often requires participation from a number of teams across the company, including where applicable, teams responsible for research; safety and alignment; product; user or customer relationships and support; intelligence, investigations and teams supporting scaled detection and enforcement; security; policy teams; global affairs; legal and privacy; and communications.
Post-deployment, we rely on monitoring, user feedback, periodic security evaluations, and incident reporting to track risk emergence over time. Material findings can be fed back into model update cycles, safety classifiers, or policy adjustments.
Questions 14 and 14A — agentic systems and controls
Yes. Some of our products can perform supported tasks using tools and a cloud browser, including reading websites and completing multi-step workflows. It pauses when it needs user input, sign-in, or confirmation. Cloud browser documentation.
We design controls to help users remain in charge of an agent’s work. In our agentic products, users can manage website permissions, review consequential actions, and take over the cloud browser. OpenAI tests for prompt injection, phishing, and unintended actions, among other things.
We also train and test the agent to resist prompt injection: attempts to make it follow malicious instructions hidden in material it encounters, such as a webpage. Monitoring helps us detect and respond to these attacks. Secure browser takeover allows users to enter credentials without exposing those inputs to the model. Together, these measures address risks that arise when an agent uses outside information or works through services where the user is signed in.
Additionally, we train the model to be aligned with human intentions, and monitor for misalignment issues. This monitoring helps us detect and respond to issues as they arise in internal and external deployment, allowing us to iterate on further safeguard and evaluation development.

We make different reporting routes available because reports can involve different kinds of problems and sensitive information. The public bounty programs provide an ongoing route for researchers to report issues that fall within the relevant program’s scope. For security incidents, the coordinated vulnerability disclosure policy directs reporters to an encrypted channel so that information can be shared securely.
The same policy brings together the rules and instructions for reporting, including the processes for vulnerabilities in third-party software and for assigning CVE identifiers. Once a report is received, further coordination depends on the organization affected, the seriousness of the issue and the information needed to investigate or fix it. This lets us keep public reporting routes accessible while handling sensitive details with the appropriate parties. Reporting instructions, program scope, and the encrypted security-incident reporting channel are available in OpenAI’s Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Policy.
The separate model-misalignment reporting framework is an employee-initiated escalation and public-disclosure process, not an external submission route. Any OpenAI employee may flag a qualifying example for investigation by the safety and alignment teams. Technical staff assess what happened, remaining uncertainties, whether disclosure is warranted, and any third-party impact; cases follow Ready for Disclosure, Minor Investigation, or Larger Investigation tracks. Disagreements about disclosure or track are referred to the Safety Advisory Group and, if necessary, OpenAI leadership. Where a third party is affected, security, legal, and responsible-disclosure obligations take precedence. We intend to give advance notice if a report would identify a third party, and publication may be delayed for security reasons. External reporters should continue using the applicable bounty and coordinated vulnerability-disclosure channels. Yes. We log and track significant reported incidents through our internal incident response processes, which include:
Triage and investigation logs
Post-incident reviews (including root cause analysis and corrective actions)
Lessons learned documentation shared with relevant internal teams
The Frontier Governance Framework describes investigations and reviews where needed to capture lessons and outstanding actions. Escalation to senior leadership and external reporting depend on the applicable incident criteria, severity and affected parties.
Separately, our model-misalignment reporting framework sets out a process to track, investigate and disclose qualifying model-behavior concerns across training, evaluation, testing and deployment. Any employee may flag an example for review by safety and alignment teams. Technical staff investigate what happened, assess uncertainties and third-party impact, and assign the case to a Ready for Disclosure, Minor Investigation or Larger Investigation track. The reporting employee is informed of the disclosure decision; unresolved disagreements about disclosure or track go to the Safety Advisory Group and, if necessary, OpenAI leadership. The process sets deadlines for investigation and disclosure, and reports document observed behavior, impacts, outstanding questions and mitigations where available; publication may precede completion of an investigation or fix. Where third parties are affected, security, legal and responsible-disclosure obligations take precedence. This framework complements existing incident-response processes and legal reporting obligations.
