Ubie is not in a position to directly manage the pre-training data of foundation models. What we manage is the quality of the medical information, evaluation data and retrieval targets that our products use.
Data quality. In our consumer-facing service we restrict sources to publicly known, reliable material - more than 50,000 medical papers and various clinical practice guidelines - and we have built a medical knowledge database covering more than 1,100 disease names. Medical information is created by in-house physicians and checked by supervising physicians, and is updated as needed in light of the latest clinical guidelines and standards of care. Each item is traceable to a cited source.
Fairness. To prevent inappropriate guidance arising from differences in disease, age, sex, expression of symptoms, or region and access to healthcare, we improve our services continuously through medical review, user feedback, feedback from customer medical institutions, and checks of evaluation data.
Assessment of limitations to generalisability. We treat instability of output quality across diverse inputs as an explicit robustness concern, in particular Japanese dialects, abbreviations and non-standard medical terminology. Benchmark or test-set performance is not read as transferring directly to real clinical language, and evaluation results are treated as valid only for the model and version tested.
Personal information. Our medical knowledge database is built from publicly known sources and does not contain patient personal data. Testing and evaluation use dummy data or anonymized and de-identified data, and personally identifiable information sent to external large language models is minimised.
Generative AI features. On the premise that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, we apply confirmation by healthcare professionals, prompt design, limitation of the intended purpose, cautionary notices on outputs, and feedback loops. Dedicated research organization. Ubie Lab, established in July 2023, advances verification of the underlying technologies and safety of generative AI, covering countermeasures against hallucination, output stability and medical accuracy. It also conducts research on policy developments and makes policy recommendations. Ubie Lab operates under the principle of achieving both innovation and safety. Publicly shared: https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000060.000048083.html
Dedicated safety function. Since January 2026 the Trust & Safety Team has carried out cross-product quality management, incident collection and classification, and pre-release review across all products. Risk assessment is performed by specialists independent of the development and business units. Not publicly disclosed as a research output, but described in this report and in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1), Column 11.
Leading a sector-wide safety standard. As leader of the Healthcare Sub-Working Group under the AISI Business Demonstration Working Group, on behalf of The Japan Digital Health Alliance (JaDHA), Ubie led the development of the Guide to Evaluation Perspectives on AI Safety in the Healthcare Sector, published in April 2026 jointly with the Japan AI Safety Institute. It sets out ten evaluation perspectives across five lifecycle phases, covering security, safety, data quality, information integrity, explainability, robustness and verifiability. Publicly shared, free of charge, and published in part in Markdown so that it can be loaded into AI services: https://aisi.go.jp/output/output_information/260402/ Ubie also led the development of the JaDHA Guide to the Utilization of Generative AI for Healthcare Providers, publicly shared at https://jadha.jp/
Data quality and representativeness. We invest continuously in a medical knowledge database built from more than 50,000 medical papers and clinical practice guidelines, covering more than 1,100 disease names, authored in-house by physicians and supervised by more than 50 physicians, with scheduled review and updating against the latest clinical guidelines. The approach and the supervision process are publicly shared: https://ubie.app/about
System performance and outcomes. In the Mayo Clinic Platform_Accelerate program we conducted performance evaluation using large-scale patient data, covering a different language and clinical-cultural context from our domestic services. Publicly shared: https://prtimes.jp/main/html/rd/p/000000175.000048083.html We also measure deployment outcomes at customer medical institutions, and publish them as case studies.
Explainability and transparency. Rather than pursuing post-hoc explanation of model internals, we invest in designs that make the basis of an output inspectable in clinical use: retrieval grounding with source citation, and the safety net structure in which the original text is displayed by default and remains retrievable alongside any AI-generated summary. Publicly described at https://ubie.life/safety
Partnerships. Safety and performance evaluation is conducted with technology partners, including our work with Google Cloud/Gemini, publicly shared on the official Google blog: https://blog.google/intl/ja-jp/company-news/technology/ubie/ We also participate in study groups as a regular member of the AI Governance Association (AIGA), where findings are shared within the consortium.
Disclosure posture. Guides, evaluation perspectives and deployment outcomes are publicly shared. Internal test criteria, prompts, guardrail configurations and specific vulnerability details are not publicly disclosed, since disclosure would reduce their effectiveness or enable exploitation.

Decision authority. Release of an AI feature is decided by the responsible product team on the basis of a cross-product review by the Trust & Safety Team. Risk assessment is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units in order to ensure objectivity. Where a material concern remains, the decision escalates to the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions), which deliberates the trade-off between AI utilization and risk together with the Generative AI Promotion Team. Other(s) (please specify): Post-deployment we identify issues early through inquiries and support from consumer users and customer medical institutions, hands-on post-deployment support, log and error monitoring, external vulnerability information, and updates to medical and AI-related guidelines. Depending on severity and scope of impact, our responses include emergency response; suspension or restriction of a feature; revision of prompts, guardrails, UI and explanatory text; updates to our medical information database; security patches; notification of customers and users; and reporting as required by law or contract. For generative AI features we maintain the premise that healthcare professionals review the outputs, and where misuse is confirmed we review training, operational guides, templates and permission settings. Root cause analysis and recurrence-prevention measures are documented as post-mortems, and we check whether the same risk exists in other features or other products.
Perform root-cause analysis and apply lessons learned to improve future development and/or deployment practices
Conduct post-deployment monitoring How records are kept. Incidents across all products are recorded and tracked in an incident management tool. Each record captures the date of occurrence, the detection channel, the scope of impact, the products involved, the root cause, the interim response, the permanent response, recurrence-prevention measures, and whether notification or reporting is required. Root cause analysis and recurrence-prevention measures are documented as post-mortems.
How records are used for follow-up. Documented findings are used to take stock of similar risks, to add test items to the criteria applied before release, for internal education, and to review policies and operating procedures. After remediation we check whether the same weakness exists in other features or other products. The Trust & Safety Team collects and classifies incidents across the organisation, which allows common issues to be distinguished from issues specific to a single product.
Escalation. For information security incidents, the person who discovers the incident reports to the Information Security Manager without delay under our Information Security Policy, and emergency measures, root cause analysis and recurrence-prevention measures follow; this is managed within our ISMS (ISO/IEC 27001) framework. Beyond that, escalation is determined by assessment rather than by a fixed numeric threshold: for each incident or vulnerability we assess the scope of impact, exploitability, the impact on medical and personal information, and whether notification is required by law or contract. Where a material concern remains, the matter is escalated to the Risk and Compliance Committee, which comprises legal, security, public relations and other functions.
External surfacing. External notification is driven by legal and contractual obligation rather than discretion. Affected customer medical institutions and pharmaceutical companies are notified, and reports are made to public authorities including the Personal Information Protection Commission where required by law. Depending on severity, the response may also include a workaround, suspension of the feature, or customer notification. Ubie integrates risk management across the AI lifecycle through three layers that operate together. (1) Two-layer governance covering promotion and risk. The Generative AI Promotion Team pursues value from AI utilization, while the Risk and Compliance Committee (legal, security, public relations and other functions) examines risk. The two share information and deliberate trade-offs, so that promotion and restraint are weighed in the same forum rather than in sequence. Risk assessment itself is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units, which separates the assessment from the incentive to ship. This structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1). (2) Cross-product quality management by the Trust & Safety Team, which reviews releases across all products, collects and classifies incidents, and distinguishes issues common to several products from issues specific to one. (3) Policies and guidelines that bind the above into repeatable practice: the Information Security Policy, the Privacy Policy, our quality guidelines, and the Ubie Trustworthy AI Policy. Escalation. Where a material concern remains after assessment, the specialists escalate to the Risk and Compliance Committee, which may decide to postpone release, limit the scope of provision, restrict the intended purpose, or require additional safeguards. Information security incidents are escalated to the Information Security Manager without delay under the Information Security Policy. Material incidents are documented as post-mortems and fed back into the test criteria applied before release. Review frequency and triggers. Practices are reviewed on a regular cycle, and additionally as needed when: a new AI or generative AI feature is introduced; an external foundation model, cloud service or data integration method changes materially; a customer medical institution's requirements are confirmed for a new deployment; a material vulnerability, incident or item of external threat intelligence is confirmed; laws or guidelines are amended, for example the AI Guidelines for Business, the AI Promotion Act, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries, the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act or the Medical Practitioners Act; or an issue is raised in an audit or by a customer. How test results feed back. Defects and risks detected are prioritised by severity and reflected in prompt revisions, additional output filters, and review of the intended scope of use. After remediation we re-test and check whether the same weakness exists in other features or other products. Distinguishing types of AI system. Generative AI features are managed on the assumption that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, so controls centre on verification: retrieval grounding with source citation, output filtering, and a human confirmation step, with the original text displayed by default and always retrievable (our "safety net structure"). Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation.Both categories are managed on the premise of a human-in-the-loop, in which a healthcare professional or a user makes the final decision. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, any future agentic capability would additionally require an explicit boundary of autonomous action and a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record.

Risk assessment itself is performed by dedicated specialists independent of the development and business units, which separates the assessment from the incentive to ship. This structure is featured as an advanced case (Column 11) in the Appendix to the METI/MIC AI Guidelines for Business (Ver. 1.1). (2) Cross-product quality management by the Trust & Safety Team, which reviews releases across all products, collects and classifies incidents, and distinguishes issues common to several products from issues specific to one. (3) Policies and guidelines that bind the above into repeatable practice: the Information Security Policy, the Privacy Policy, our quality guidelines, and the Ubie Trustworthy AI Policy. Escalation. Where a material concern remains after assessment, the specialists escalate to the Risk and Compliance Committee, which may decide to postpone release, limit the scope of provision, restrict the intended purpose, or require additional safeguards. Information security incidents are escalated to the Information Security Manager without delay under the Information Security Policy. Material incidents are documented as post-mortems and fed back into the test criteria applied before release. Review frequency and triggers. Practices are reviewed on a regular cycle, and additionally as needed when: a new AI or generative AI feature is introduced; an external foundation model, cloud service or data integration method changes materially; a customer medical institution's requirements are confirmed for a new deployment; a material vulnerability, incident or item of external threat intelligence is confirmed; laws or guidelines are amended, for example the AI Guidelines for Business, the AI Promotion Act, the Act on the Protection of Personal Information, the Two Guidelines from Three Ministries, the Pharmaceuticals and Medical Devices Act or the Medical Practitioners Act; or an issue is raised in an audit or by a customer. How test results feed back. Defects and risks detected are prioritised by severity and reflected in prompt revisions, additional output filters, and review of the intended scope of use. After remediation we re-test and check whether the same weakness exists in other features or other products. Distinguishing types of AI system. Generative AI features are managed on the assumption that outputs of external foundation models may contain bias or hallucination, so controls centre on verification: retrieval grounding with source citation, output filtering, and a human confirmation step, with the original text displayed by default and always retrievable (our "safety net structure"). Agentic AI systems that plan or act to a partial extent are under evaluation.Both categories are managed on the premise of a human-in-the-loop, in which a healthcare professional or a user makes the final decision. Because an error in the medical domain can be irreversible, any future agentic capability would additionally require an explicit boundary of autonomous action and a human decision point before any action affecting a patient or a medical record.
